previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: A man with non-ischemic dilated cardiomyopathy, COPD, and a history of cocaine dependence was admitted for acute respiratory distress and hypoxia. He presented with progressive shortness of breath, cough with yellowish sputum, and diffuse chest tightness, despite denying recent crack use. Initial evaluation revealed bilateral lung opacities on imaging, elevated BNP, and leukocytosis. He was treated for both acute on chronic systolic heart failure and crack cocaine pneumonitis. Aggressive diuresis was initiated but provided limited respiratory improvement, leading to a diagnosis of predominant pneumonitis. He was started on steroids and antibiotics, with gradual improvement in oxygenation and lung findings. His diabetes was managed with increased insulin due to steroid use, later tapered back. He was transitioned from metoprolol to carvedilol, and lisinopril was reduced. He was discharged home after eight days, ambulating independently on room air, with a plan for outpatient follow-up and nicotine replacement therapy.

Brief Hospital Course:
In the MICU, patient was treated with solumedrol, oxygen, and 
lasix for presumed pneumonitis and CHF exacerbation.  He 
improved and was transferred to the floor.  

Upon transfer to the floor, the patient required supplemental 
oxygen to maintain oxygen saturation greater than 92%. He was 
hemodynamically stable with a sinus tachycardia in the high 
___. The patients antibiotics were discontinued as there 
was no evidence that he had a bacterial pneumonia: no white 
blood cell count, no fever, rapid improvement in symptoms with 
steroids. Upon discontinuation of his antibiotics, he remained 
afebrile. He was treated with supportive therapy for 
crack-cocaine pneumonititis with nebulizers and a 4 day course 
of oral prednisone. His hospitalization on the floor was 
uneventful. He spent most of the day watching TV and talking on 
the telephone. Each day his oxygenation improved until the day 
of discharge where he was able to ambulate with a oxygen 
saturation above 90%. 

At that point, he was discharged with an appointment at the 
___ Dual Diagnosis Partial Day Program on ___. Psychiatry 
recommended stopping his Zoloft because they felt that he was 
not clinically depressed and Zoloft was not indicated. The 
patient was continued on his home medications (lasix 40mg was 
restarted) and given a prescription to attend ___ 
rehabilitation.

1.Cessation of smoking (crack and tobacco) 
2.Outpatient Dual Diagnosis therapy

for prevention of sudden cardiac death.

radiology_notes.text:
INDICATION:  ___ male with shortness of breath.  Evaluate for evidence
of CHF.

COMPARISON:  Multiple chest radiographs, latest one on ___.

TECHNIQUE:  Portable chest radiograph.

FINDINGS:  There are diffuse airspace opacities spanning nearly the totality
of both lungs, with some sparing of an ill-defined region in the right upper
lung.  The cardiomediastinal and hilar contours are unremarkable.  There is no
pleural effusion or pneumothorax.

IMPRESSION:  Bilateral opacities occupying nearly the totality of the lungs
consistent with acute pulmonary edema. Diffuse reactive inflammatory process
such as pneumonitis or infection cannot be excluded.

SINGLE FRONTAL VIEW OF THE CHEST.

REASON FOR EXAM:  cocaine pneumonitis likely and CHF.

Comparison is made with prior study performed a day earlier.

Cardiomediastinal contours are unchanged.  Extensive bilateral lung opacities
have improved consistent with improving pulmonary edema or acute pneumonitis. 
There are no new lung opacities, pneumothorax, or enlarging pleural effusions.
